public_rationale: The archived CNN benchmark supports concern about source fidelity: its best reported model still had a 15% error rate. That does not establish a general inability to check outputs, and research on explicit fact-checking supplies a qualification. The USD 500 billion assertion remains unverified. Available investment and data-centre figures measure different things, and the claim supplies no accounting basis. The compound claim therefore cannot be scored supported or contradicted.
limitations: The money component has an unknown accounting basis.
The 60-question benchmark is small and uses an automated checking system.
A grounding error rate is not automatically a self-verification failure rate.
The cumulative cost window is approximate; contemporary capability is assessed using pre-post reports.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: LLM technology, having cost about half a trillion dollars, cannot reliably check its output against Wikipedia or a supplied article.

statement.excerpt: If I can be blunt, it is an absolute embarrassment that a technology that has collectively cost about half a trillion dollars can’t do something as basic as (reliably) check its output against wikipedia or a CNN article that is handed on a silver plattter.
statement.document_title: Why DO large language models hallucinate?

from_speaker: technology that has collectively cost about half a trillion dollars
can’t do something as basic as (reliably) check its output
our_interpretation: Assess the spending and reliability assertions together; exclude the judgement that the situation is embarrassing.
Read the money figure as approximately USD 500 billion in cumulative costs attributable to LLM technology, not funding raised, valuations or future commitments.
The surrounding post describes roughly eight years of expenditure. Use 2017 as the approximate starting year, with January 1 only as an inclusive year boundary, and end at the post date.
For the ongoing capability assertion, use the latest pre-post evidence, including the April 2025 report linked by Marcus. Older capability studies are context.

Read reliable checking as dependable detection or avoidance of factual mismatches against supplied sources, not perfect performance on every possible input. No numerical reliability threshold is imposed.
criteria.support_condition: A defined, non-duplicative accounting of cumulative LLM costs supports approximately USD 500 billion by the post, and contemporary evaluations show material failures when checking against available or supplied sources.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Comparable expenditure records place cumulative costs clearly outside a defensible approximation to USD 500 billion, or representative contemporary evaluations establish dependable source checking under the claimed conditions.

evidence.excerpt: Our benchmark revealed that OpenAI GPT-4.5 has the lowest hallucination rate (i.e. highest accuracy rate) of 15%.
evidence.explanation: The archived report describes 60 CNN-based questions per model and a best reported error rate of 15%, supporting the narrower concern about source fidelity. It tests answering from supplied material rather than a separate self-verification procedure and cannot settle the spending assertion.

evidence.excerpt: Training on this data teaches models to check each fact in the claim and recognize synthesis of information across sentences.
evidence.explanation: MiniCheck directly studies checking generated claims against grounding documents and reports models reaching GPT-4-level performance. This qualifies a reading of complete incapability, but does not establish a reliability threshold or the performance of all systems in April 2025.

evidence.excerpt:
Private investment in generative AI reached $33.9 billion in 2024, up 18.7% from 2023
and over 8.5 times higher than 2022 levels.
evidence.explanation: This measures private investment in generative AI during one calendar year. It neither supports nor contradicts cumulative expenditure on LLM technology.

evidence.excerpt:
Investment is surging in new data centres and the capital-intensive IT equipment used for
training and running AI models.
evidence.publisher: International Energy Agency; European Commission-hosted copy
evidence.explanation: The section estimates annual data-centre investment exceeding USD 500 billion in 2024. Its infrastructure scope and annual period differ from cumulative LLM costs, so the similar number does not validate Marcus's figure.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: A documented cumulative LLM expenditure estimate with clear scope and accounting, together with representative pre-post tests of explicit checking against supplied sources under a stated reliability criterion.
